set.stem: A 25-year-old man with a diagnosis of heart failure has used a wheelchair for many years and has severe scoliosis. His ECG shows tall R waves in V1 and V2 with deep Q waves in V5 and V6, and echocardiography shows severe global left ventricular dysfunction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked dystrophin deficiency in boys, causing loss of ambulation in early adolescence, scoliosis and a progressive dilated cardiomyopathy that is a leading cause of death. Fibrosis of the posterobasal and lateral LV wall gives the characteristic ECG of tall R waves in V1–V2 and deep narrow Q waves in the lateral leads. ALS starts in adulthood, ASD does not cause LV failure, and chronic thromboembolic disease affects the right heart. Management includes ACE inhibitors or ARBs and beta-blockers, started early, and cardiac surveillance with MRI.

Most familial cardiomyopathies (hypertrophic, and many dilated and arrhythmogenic forms) are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, commonly through missense mutations in sarcomeric genes such as MYH7 and MYBPC3 (in HCM) or in genes such as TTN, LMNA and desmosomal genes. X-linked forms (Duchenne and Becker dystrophies, Fabry disease, Danon disease) and autosomal recessive forms are less common. First-degree relatives should be offered genetic counselling, cascade genetic testing and clinical screening with ECG and echocardiography.

set.stem: A 45-year-old man with obesity presents with several months of breathlessness, fatigue and a nocturnal cough. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a globally reduced ejection fraction of 25%. Which blood test is routinely recommended in all patients with newly diagnosed heart failure to identify a reversible cause?
options: Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme
Anti-nuclear antibodies
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Coxsackie virus serology
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
set.explanation: Both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism can cause or worsen heart failure and are readily reversible, so thyroid function is part of the routine initial blood tests in new heart failure, along with full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, liver function, natriuretic peptide and iron studies (ferritin and transferrin saturation). Serum ACE, autoantibodies, ESR and viral serology are not routine and are requested only when a specific cause (sarcoidosis, connective tissue disease, myocarditis) is suspected; viral serology rarely changes management.

why: Under current ESC guidance, iron studies and cardiac MRI are also class I recommendations, so the original options gave several defensible answers; stem and distractors rewritten

set.stem: A 22-year-old student presents with lethargy and fatigue 3 days after a viral upper respiratory illness. He is obtunded, tachycardic and hypotensive, with cool peripheries and a raised jugular venous pressure. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30% with mild mitral regurgitation, and endomyocardial biopsy shows lymphocytic myocarditis. Which of the following statements about his prognosis and treatment is true?
set.explanation: Fulminant lymphocytic (viral) myocarditis presents dramatically with cardiogenic shock, but if the patient is supported through the acute phase, the prognosis is good: most survive, and LV function often recovers fully over weeks to months. Aggressive inotropic support and mechanical circulatory support (such as ECMO or a ventricular assist device) as a bridge to recovery are therefore warranted, rather than immediate transplant listing. Routine immunosuppression has not been shown to improve survival in lymphocytic viral myocarditis, and anti-heart antibody titres do not guide prognosis.

set.stem: A 42-year-old woman with autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is brought in after collapsing at home. She reports several days of worsening lethargy and chest discomfort. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%, and endomyocardial biopsy shows diffuse inflammatory infiltrates with multinucleated giant cells and myocyte necrosis. Which of the following statements about her diagnosis is true?
options: Most patients with this form of cardiomyopathy recover with supportive care
Steroids alone are highly effective in treating this form of cardiomyopathy
The course is often rapidly progressive, with deterioration requiring urgent transplantation
Ventricular tachyarrhythmias are rare in this disease
None of the above is true
set.explanation: Giant cell myocarditis is a rare autoimmune myocarditis of young and middle-aged adults, associated with other autoimmune diseases such as thyroiditis and inflammatory bowel disease. It progresses rapidly with heart failure, heart block and frequent ventricular tachycardia, and without treatment median survival is only a few months. Combined immunosuppression (steroids with ciclosporin or other agents) improves survival but many patients still need mechanical support or urgent transplantation, and recurrence in the graft is possible.

Anthracycline (e.g. doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity is dose-dependent and irreversible, caused by free-radical injury and topoisomerase-2β-mediated myocyte death, with risk rising steeply above a cumulative doxorubicin dose of about 400–450 mg/m². Risk is increased by mediastinal or chest radiotherapy, pre-existing heart disease or hypertension, extremes of age, and concurrent or sequential trastuzumab (whose own cardiotoxicity is usually reversible). Patients need baseline and serial LVEF (with strain imaging and troponin), and dexrazoxane or liposomal preparations can reduce risk.

set.stem: A 32-year-old man presents with chest pain after a week of coryza, cough, fever and muscle aches. The pain is constant, radiates to his left shoulder, and is worse lying flat and on deep inspiration. There is a scratchy extracardiac sound with three components per heartbeat. His ECG is shown, and troponin I is undetectable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Aspirin 75 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 80 mg daily
High-dose aspirin (750 mg–1 g every 8 hours) plus colchicine, with proton pump inhibitor cover
Heparin, aspirin and clopidogrel with immediate coronary angiography
Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks, then tapered over 2 months
Thrombolysis with alteplase
set.explanation: Pleuritic, positional pain after a viral illness, a three-component pericardial friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression (and PR elevation in aVR) on the ECG and a normal troponin indicate acute viral pericarditis. First-line treatment is high-dose aspirin or an NSAID (such as ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours) with gastroprotection, plus colchicine for 3 months, which halves recurrence. Steroids are second-line because they increase recurrences, and antiplatelet regimens, angiography or thrombolysis are for acute coronary syndromes; an echocardiogram is still recommended to look for an effusion.

why: 'Next step' made transthoracic echocardiography (recommended in all suspected pericarditis) also defensible; stem now asks for treatment, colchicine added to the aspirin option, echo option replaced with thrombolysis
Same idea as 39 Blocks peri-0004 (acute pericarditis followed by hypotension and a raised JVP: cardiac tamponade)

set.explanation: In tamponade the total volume of the heart is fixed by the tense pericardial fluid, so the two ventricles compete for space. On inspiration, venous return to the right heart increases (tricuspid inflow velocity rises by more than 40%) and the septum shifts to the left, reducing LV filling, mitral inflow velocity, LV stroke volume and systolic blood pressure. A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg on inspiration is pulsus paradoxus, and exaggerated respiratory variation in Doppler inflow velocities supports the echocardiographic diagnosis.

Features favouring pericarditis over MI include widespread concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation not confined to one coronary territory, PR-segment depression, no reciprocal ST depression (except in aVR and V1), no pathological Q waves, and T-wave inversion occurring only after the ST segments have returned to baseline. ST elevation in V2 occurs in both conditions (and as a normal variant), so it does not help to distinguish them.

Mediastinal radiotherapy is a recognised cause of constrictive pericarditis, in which a thickened, rigid pericardium allows rapid early diastolic filling that stops abruptly (the pericardial knock and dip-and-plateau pressure trace). Diuretics relieve congestion only temporarily, and the definitive treatment of chronic constriction is surgical pericardiectomy, although outcomes after radiation-induced constriction are worse because of associated myocardial, valve and coronary damage. Pericardiocentesis treats effusion, not constriction, and transplantation and valve replacement are not indicated.

set.stem: A 45-year-old man with a 3-month history of fevers, symmetrical arthralgia and fatigue develops sudden left hand weakness that resolves within 1 hour. Echocardiography shows a solitary 2-cm pedunculated mass in the left atrium arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: A pedunculated left atrial mass attached to the fossa ovalis region, with constitutional symptoms (from interleukin-6 release) and a transient ischaemic attack from embolism, is an atrial myxoma. It should be removed surgically without delay because of the risk of further embolism and mitral obstruction; histology of the excised tumour confirms the diagnosis. Biopsy is unnecessary and risks embolisation, the appearance is not that of a vegetation (which sits on valve leaflets), and autoimmune serology or a PET scan would only delay treatment.

Secondary tumours of the heart are 20–40 times commoner than primary tumours. Melanoma has the highest propensity to metastasise to the heart (cardiac involvement in over half of those dying of it), while in absolute numbers lung and breast cancer, lymphoma and leukaemia are the commonest sources because they are frequent. Glioblastoma rarely spreads outside the central nervous system. Cardiac metastases most often involve the pericardium, causing effusion and tamponade.

set.stem: At a children's baseball game, a 12-year-old catcher is struck in the chest by a foul ball and immediately collapses in cardiac arrest. Which intervention is most critical for his survival?
set.explanation: Commotio cordis is sudden cardiac arrest caused by a blunt, non-penetrating blow to the precordium during the vulnerable upslope of the T wave, which triggers ventricular fibrillation in a structurally normal heart. Survival depends on immediate CPR and early defibrillation, ideally with an AED within a few minutes. The heart is not structurally injured, so coronary intervention or surgery is not needed, and survival is now much better when defibrillation is prompt.

set.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes asks about her future risk of heart attack and stroke. What is the most common cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus?
set.explanation: Cardiovascular disease causes most deaths in adults with type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease is the leading single cause, occurring at 2–4 times the rate in people without diabetes and often with atypical or silent ischaemia. Stroke is also increased but less frequent than coronary death, and renal failure and infection account for smaller proportions. This is why statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation and SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists with proven cardiovascular benefit are central to diabetes care.

set.stem: A 49-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with high-output heart failure. After treatment, his symptoms and left ventricular size improve rapidly. Which treatment most likely produced this improvement?
set.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, common with heavy alcohol use and malnutrition, causes wet beriberi: peripheral vasodilatation with a high-output state, oedema and biventricular failure. Replacing thiamine produces a rapid and dramatic improvement, often within days. By contrast, alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy is a low-output state that improves more slowly with abstinence. Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency causes anaemia but not this picture, and thiamine should always be given before glucose in malnourished patients who drink heavily.

set.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair and leg swelling. Her TSH is 79.4 mU/L. Which cardiovascular measurement is NOT expected to decrease?
set.explanation: Thyroid hormone increases heart rate, contractility and blood volume and lowers systemic vascular resistance, so in hypothyroidism heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output fall, systemic resistance rises (causing diastolic hypertension), and pulse pressure narrows. On the ECG there is sinus bradycardia, low voltage (sometimes from pericardial effusion) and QT prolongation, which increases rather than decreases. Thyroxine replacement reverses these changes, but should be started at a low dose in older patients or those with ischaemic heart disease.

Atherogenesis begins when LDL particles enter and are retained in the arterial intima by binding to proteoglycans, especially at branch points with disturbed flow. The trapped lipoproteins then undergo oxidative modification, which activates the endothelium to express adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1; monocytes are recruited, become macrophages and take up modified LDL through scavenger receptors to form foam cells (the fatty streak). Smooth-muscle migration and fibrous cap formation follow, which is why lowering LDL is central to prevention.

In early atherosclerosis the artery undergoes compensatory outward (positive) remodelling, with the plaque growing abluminally, so the lumen is preserved until the plaque occupies about 40% of the area within the internal elastic lamina (Glagov phenomenon). Many plaques therefore never cause stenosis or symptoms, although non-stenotic lipid-rich plaques can rupture and cause acute coronary syndromes. Total occlusion does not always cause infarction if collaterals have developed.

set.stem: Under the 2013 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline (whose statin benefit groups were retained in 2018), all of the following are statin benefit groups EXCEPT:
options: All individuals with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
Individuals with a raised high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol or ASCVD risk
Individuals with LDL cholesterol of 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) or more without a secondary cause
Individuals aged 40–75 years without ASCVD or diabetes, with LDL 1.8–4.9 mmol/L (70–189 mg/dL) and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or more
Individuals aged 40–75 years with diabetes but no ASCVD, with LDL 1.8–4.9 mmol/L (70–189 mg/dL)
set.explanation: The four statin benefit groups are clinical ASCVD, LDL of 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) or more (often familial hypercholesterolaemia), diabetes aged 40–75 years, and primary prevention aged 40–75 years with a 10-year risk of 7.5% or more. A raised hs-CRP alone is not an indication; in the 2018 guideline it is only a risk enhancer that can tip the decision in intermediate-risk patients. In the UK, NICE uses a 10-year QRISK3 score of 10% or more for primary prevention with atorvastatin 20 mg.

set.stem: A 50-year-old man with obesity attends his annual check-up. He has no known vascular disease and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 6%. His lipid profile shows total cholesterol 5.7 mmol/L (220 mg/dL), triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L (283 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol 0.75 mmol/L (29 mg/dL) and LDL cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (132 mg/dL). He is concerned about his low HDL. Which intervention aimed at his low HDL has been shown to lower his cardiovascular risk?
options: A peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-δ agonist
A cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitor
Fenofibrate
Nicotinic acid
Weight loss and regular physical activity
set.explanation: Low HDL is a marker of risk, but drugs that raise HDL have not reduced cardiovascular events: CETP inhibitors (torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, evacetrapib) and niacin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) failed, fibrates did not reduce events on top of statins (ACCORD-Lipid), and PPAR-δ agonists remain experimental. Weight loss, regular aerobic exercise and stopping smoking raise HDL modestly, lower triglycerides and improve overall cardiometabolic risk, so lifestyle change is the right approach, with statins used according to overall risk and LDL.

set.explanation: The major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand are heart rate, contractility and wall stress (by Laplace's law, proportional to pressure times radius divided by wall thickness, reflecting both preload and afterload). Heart rhythm itself is not a primary determinant, although arrhythmias act through changes in rate. Anti-anginal drugs work on these factors: beta-blockers and rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers reduce rate and contractility, and nitrates reduce preload and hence wall stress.

set.stem: During an exercise stress test, how does the normal heart meet its increased oxygen demand?
set.explanation: The myocardium already extracts about 70–75% of the oxygen from coronary blood at rest, so extraction cannot rise much, and increased demand must be met by increasing coronary flow. This occurs by metabolic dilatation of the intramyocardial resistance arterioles (mediated by adenosine, nitric oxide, hypoxia and potassium), while the large epicardial arteries act mainly as conduits. The myocardium is not supplied from blood in the ventricular chambers, and diastole, when most coronary flow occurs, shortens as heart rate rises.

set.stem: A man develops angina during an exercise stress test. Which of the following biochemical changes would NOT be expected in his ischaemic myocardium?
set.explanation: When oxygen supply falls short of demand, myocytes switch from aerobic to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate and hydrogen ions, so intracellular pH falls rather than rises. Stores of ATP and creatine phosphate are depleted, ATP-dependent pumps fail so cytosolic calcium rises (impairing relaxation first, then contraction), and potassium leaks out of the cells, contributing to ST-segment changes and arrhythmias. This sequence, the ischaemic cascade, explains why diastolic dysfunction precedes ECG changes and angina.

set.stem: Which of the following is an unusual site for radiation of anginal pain?
set.explanation: Anginal pain is typically retrosternal and radiates to the left arm, both arms, the neck and jaw (including the teeth), the epigastrium, the back and the interscapular region. Radiation to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericarditis, because the phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragmatic pericardium, and it is unusual for myocardial ischaemia.

set.stem: A 70-year-old man with mild chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus and heart failure is admitted with reduced urine output, weakness and breathlessness. He takes several medications but cannot remember their names. Blood results are pending, and his ECG is shown. Based on the information available, what is the best initial step in management?
set.explanation: The ECG shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves with flattened P waves, typical of hyperkalaemia, likely from renal impairment plus drugs such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone or NSAIDs. With ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate (10 mL of 10%, repeated if needed) is given first to stabilise the myocardial membrane within minutes, without waiting for laboratory results. This is followed by IV insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol to shift potassium into cells, and then potassium removal (binders, diuretics or dialysis); bicarbonate is reserved for acidosis, and hypertonic saline has no role.

set.stem: A surgical colleague asks you to review a 54-year-old woman with ECG abnormalities the day after a subtotal thyroidectomy for toxic multinodular goitre. Her only medication is fentanyl for postoperative pain. She has no history of syncope and no family history of sudden cardiac death. Examination is unremarkable apart from a clean incision at the base of the neck. Her ECG is shown. What is the best next step?
set.explanation: The ECG shows a prolonged QT (QTc 0.52 s) caused by lengthening of the ST segment with a normal T wave, the pattern of hypocalcaemia. After thyroidectomy this is most often due to parathyroid damage or devascularisation (transient or permanent hypoparathyroidism), so ionised calcium should be measured and IV calcium gluconate given if it is low or the patient is symptomatic. Magnesium is used to treat torsades de pointes, brain CT is for suspected intracranial events, and auditory testing is for congenital long QT with deafness (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome); a QTc of 0.52 s is never normal.

The fourth heart sound is produced by atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle (e.g. hypertensive LV hypertrophy), so it occurs in late diastole just after the P wave and before the QRS complex. The first heart sound coincides with the QRS complex, the second with the end of the T wave, and a third heart sound occurs in early diastole after the T wave. An S4 cannot occur in atrial fibrillation because there is no effective atrial contraction.
